options.A: Shake the roll vigorously in the air until the water stops dripping
options.B: Leave the roll soaking in the water until ready for the next layer
options.C: Gently squeeze both ends to remove excess water without twisting
options.D: Wring the roll tightly like a wet towel to make it completely dry

explanation: Never twist the roll because it messes up the plaster structure! A gentle squeeze from the ends gets rid of extra water safely. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h4)

question: A patient with a new leg cast complains of severe, throbbing pain that pain meds aren't helping. What is your first step?

options.A: Apply a heating pad over the cast to relax the cramped calf muscles
options.B: Administer a stronger dose of narcotic pain medication immediately
options.C: Elevate the leg above heart level and wait another two hours to see
options.D: Perform a neurovascular assessment of the toes and check for cast tightness

explanation: Unrelieved pain is a big red flag for dangerous swelling! Always check circulation, motion, and sensation (neurovascular check) right away. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h5)

question: How should a freshly applied Plaster of Paris cast be supported while it dries?

options.A: Covered tightly with heavy warm blankets to trap heat
options.B: Suspended vertically by a rope attached to the ceiling
options.C: Lying directly flat on a hard wooden examination table
options.D: Resting on soft pillows with open air circulation

explanation: Soft pillows cradle the wet cast and support its shape without pressing flat, damaging spots into the drying plaster. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h5)

question: What causes compartment syndrome in a patient wearing a rigid cast?

options.A: Bacterial infection develops under the padding and destroys the muscle tissue
options.B: The chemical powder used in the plaster seeps into the bloodstream and causes clotting
options.C: Swelling trapped inside a non-expanding cast puts extreme pressure on blood vessels and nerves
options.D: The patient fails to move their fingers or toes enough, causing poor circulation

explanation: Because a plaster cast can't stretch, any swelling inside builds up high pressure that squeezes the blood vessels and nerves. This is a medical emergency! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a classic sign of compartment syndrome?

options.A: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes in the limb
options.B: Numbness and tingling sensations in the digits
options.C: Absent or very weak pulses in the affected extremity
options.D: Severe pain that does not respond to painkillers

explanation: Think of the 'Ps' of compartment syndrome: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis. Hyperactive reflexes don't belong on that list! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h6)

question: A patient with an arm cast complains of an intense itch deep inside. What advice should you give?

options.A: Pour a small amount of baby oil down the cast opening to soothe the skin
options.B: Insert a clean knitting needle gently down the side to scratch the itchy spot
options.C: Use a cool hair dryer breeze directed into the cast opening to relieve itching
options.D: Submerge the entire arm in warm soapy water until the itching stops

explanation: A cool breeze from a hair dryer is a safe trick to ease itching. Never stick objects inside the cast—they can break skin or get stuck! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h7)

question: What happens to a Plaster of Paris cast if it gets wet?

options.A: It dries out and becomes twice as hard as before
options.B: It shrinks tightly and cuts off blood circulation
options.C: It changes color from white to bright yellow
options.D: It softens, weakens, and loses its structural shape

explanation: Unlike fiberglass, traditional plaster will break down and lose its strength when exposed to water. Keep it dry! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why is an oscillating cast saw safe against human skin during cast removal?

options.A: The saw is powered by low-voltage batteries that stop when touching skin
options.B: The metal blade is coated with a special chemical that repels human tissue
options.C: The blade vibrates back and forth instead of spinning in a continuous circle
options.D: The vibration creates a cooling effect that hardens the skin temporarily

explanation: The oscillating (back-and-forth) motion cuts right through hard plaster, but just bounces safely off soft, stretchy skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h8)

question: What does the skin usually look like right after a long-term cast is removed?

options.A: Bright red, inflamed, and completely covered in blisters
options.B: Dry, scaly, and pale with accumulated dead skin cells
options.C: Deeply tanned from being shielded from outdoor sunlight
options.D: Oily, moist, and smelling strongly of fresh antiseptic lotion

explanation: Because dead skin cells couldn't shed normally while trapped in the cast, the skin looks dry and flaky when the cast finally comes off. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T5#GNS221_U1_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary physical characteristic of a stockinette used in orthopedics?

options.A: Adhesive on one side
options.B: Rigid and non-stretchable
options.C: Seamless and tube-like
options.D: Waterproof and plastic

explanation: A stockinette is manufactured as a continuous knitted tube without seams to prevent localized skin irritation under casts. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is cotton commonly used as the material for orthopedic stockinettes?

options.A: It acts as a strong primary weight-bearing layer
options.B: It chemically hardens when exposed to water
options.C: It provides permanent waterproofing for the limb
options.D: It allows skin breathability and reduces moisture

explanation: Cotton fibers absorb minimal moisture and allow air circulation, which helps maintain skin integrity under a cast. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h1)

question: The main purpose of a stockinette under a cast is to...

options.A: speed up the drying time of plaster
options.B: permanently immobilize the joint bones
options.C: administer topical antibiotics to wounds
options.D: protect the skin from abrasive materials

explanation: The fabric creates a smooth barrier that shields the epidermis from direct contact with rough casting tape. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h2)

question: A patient complains of a scratching sensation inside a newly applied forearm cast. What role did a poorly applied stockinette likely play?

options.A: Excessive padding causing a compartment syndrome
options.B: Inadequate venous return from tight wrapping
options.C: Chemical burns from synthetic resin drying
options.D: Failure to cover rough edges of the plaster

explanation: If the stockinette does not extend far enough past the cast edges, rough plaster or fiberglass can directly chafe the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which material choice is best suited for a modern waterproof cast system?

options.A: Raw linen
options.B: Pure cotton
options.C: Synthetic fibers
options.D: Heavy wool

explanation: Synthetic stockinettes paired with specialized padding allow water to drain freely away from the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h3)

question: A key advantage of standard cotton stockinette over synthetic alternatives is its...

options.A: high resistance to stretching out of shape
options.B: permanent waterproof chemical treatment
options.C: superior comfort and absorbent quality
options.D: ability to repel all body fluids entirely

explanation: Cotton offers high patient comfort and naturally absorbs normal skin perspiration. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why must a nurse ensure a stockinette is free of wrinkles before casting?

options.A: Wrinkles prevent the plaster from hardening properly in time
options.B: Wrinkles create high-pressure areas that can cause skin breakdown
options.C: Wrinkles trap excessive heat and cause immediate chemical burns
options.D: Wrinkles make the finished cast too heavy for the patient

explanation: Any crease or fold trapped under a rigid cast exerts uneven pressure against the skin, risking ischemia and ulceration. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h4)

question: How far beyond the intended cast boundaries should the stockinette ideally extend?

options.A: Covering the entire opposite limb
options.B: Exactly at the cast edge line
options.C: Only at the upper proximal end
options.D: Several inches on both ends

explanation: Extending the fabric past the cast edges allows the nurse to fold it back, creating a smooth, padded border. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is a major risk if a stockinette is applied with excessive tension?

options.A: Rapid dissolution of the cast material
options.B: Permanent discoloration of the outer cast
options.C: Impaired circulation to the limb
options.D: Immediate infection of deep muscle tissue

explanation: A stockinette that is too narrow or pulled too tightly can restrict blood flow like a tourniquet. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h5)

question: What should a nurse check first when evaluating a limb encased in a stockinette and plaster cast?

options.A: Distal pulse and capillary refill
options.B: The exact brand of the casting tape
options.C: The length of the excess folded fabric
options.D: The weight of the dried plaster shell

explanation: Neurovascular checks prioritize blood flow and nerve function distal to the immobilized area. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h5)

question: What warning should nurses give patients regarding itching under a stockinette and cast?

options.A: Use a wooden stick for safe scratching relief
options.B: Pour warm water down the tube to cool the skin
options.C: Never insert objects inside the cast to scratch
options.D: Apply greasy oil directly onto the fabric edge

explanation: Inserting foreign items can break fragile skin hidden beneath the layers, leading to severe localized infection. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which sign reported by a patient requires immediate clinical investigation of the cast area?

options.A: A foul odor or hot spot on the cast
options.B: Itching relieved by cool air from a fan
options.C: Dry skin flakes near the open cast edge
options.D: Normal mild muscle weakness from rest

explanation: Foul odors and localized warmth often indicate underlying skin breakdown, pressure necrosis, or infection. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T6#GNS221_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of using orthopedic traction?

options.A: To apply a pulling force to align bones and reduce spasms
options.B: To completely immobilize the patient without using any bed sheets
options.C: To permanently replace damaged joint cartilage without surgery
options.D: To deliver strong local pain medication directly into a fracture

explanation: Traction uses a steady pull on body parts to restore bone alignment, stretch tight muscles, and ease painful spasms before definitive repair. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h1)

question: How does skeletal traction differ fundamentally from skin traction?

options.A: Skeletal traction avoids any risk of infection because no hardware is used
options.B: Skeletal traction uses much lighter weights for short periods
options.C: Skeletal traction attaches directly to bone using metal pins
options.D: Skeletal traction relies entirely on elastic bandages wrapped loosely

explanation: Skeletal traction requires surgical insertion of pins or wires into the bone to handle heavier weights over a longer duration, unlike skin-surface methods. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h1)

question: What should the nurse do if the weights attached to skeletal traction accidentally rest on the floor?

options.A: Leave them on the floor to give the patient a rest
options.B: Lift and rehang the weights so they hang freely
options.C: Remove the traction ropes permanently from the bed frame
options.D: Add an extra five kilograms of weight to compensate

explanation: Traction weights must never touch the floor because ground support removes the pulling force, leading to loss of bone alignment and sudden muscle spasms. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h2)

question: A patient in skin traction complains of severe leg spasms, and the nurse sees the rope is caught on the pulley wheel. What is the best first step?

options.A: Realign the rope smoothly into the center of the pulley groove
options.B: Cut the traction tape immediately to release all skin pressure
options.C: Administer a stronger pain pill and wait for relief
options.D: Raise the head of the bed high

explanation: You've got this! When a rope slips, the weights stop pulling correctly, which causes muscle spasms. Just pop the rope back into the groove to fix the tension right away. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which sign tells you that a limb in traction has poor blood flow?

options.A: The ability to wiggle all toes easily on command
options.B: Cold toes and a slow capillary refill over four seconds
options.C: Warm skin and a strong pulse in the foot
options.D: Normal pink coloration of the nail beds

explanation: Great job thinking through circulation checks! Cold toes and sluggish refill are classic warning signs that pressure or swelling is slowing down blood flow. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h3)

question: Why must you always ask a patient in traction if they feel numbness or tingling in their toes?

options.A: It confirms the skeletal pins are securely anchored
options.B: These symptoms point to early nerve pressure or poor blood supply
options.C: It proves their pain medication dosage is correct
options.D: It helps calculate their daily calcium levels

explanation: Spot on! Numbness and tingling are your early warning bells for pinched nerves or reduced circulation, letting you act before tissue damage happens. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for performing meticulous pin site care on a patient with skeletal traction?

options.A: To encourage faster healing of torn skin ligaments
options.B: To keep the traction weights from touching the floor
options.C: To stop the metal pins from slipping out of the bone
options.D: To prevent dangerous bone infections like osteomyelitis

explanation: Pin sites create a direct open route from the environment to the bone, making rigorous sterile cleaning vital to stop bacterial invasion. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which finding around a skeletal traction pin site means you need to call the doctor right away?

options.A: A small amount of clear dried crust around the metal entry point
options.B: The metal pin is visibly loose or wobbling
options.C: Mild skin redness close to the pin
options.D: Clear fluid drainage during the first day

explanation: You're doing great! Pins need to stay rock-solid in the bone. A loose pin messes up the whole traction setup and always needs a doctor's attention. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why are deep breathing exercises so important for a patient stuck on bed rest in traction?

options.A: They relax tight muscles to stop spasms
options.B: They stimulate blood flow inside the deep calf veins
options.C: They expand the lungs fully to prevent mucus buildup and collapse
options.D: They increase the pulling force of the traction weights

explanation: Thinking like a real nurse! Lying in bed slows down breathing, which can cause lung issues. Deep breaths keep the tiny air sacs open and clear out mucus. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h5)

question: A patient on long-term traction complains of sudden calf pain, swelling, and warmth in their other leg. What should you suspect?

options.A: Normal muscle fatigue
options.B: Superficial skin abrasion
options.C: Deep vein thrombosis
options.D: Early pin site infection

explanation: Spot on! When patients can't move around much, blood flow slows down, putting them at risk for a blood clot (DVT) in the calf. Always stay alert for this! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is a helpful nursing action to ease a patient's anxiety about being stuck in traction?

options.A: Explain the equipment clearly and keep their call bell close by
options.B: Take away all entertainment to help them sleep
options.C: Promise to take the traction off whenever they get bored
options.D: Tell family members not to visit so the room stays quiet

explanation: You've got this! Knowing how the equipment works and knowing help is just a button press away builds huge trust and comfort for the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why is checking on the emotional wellbeing of a patient in long-term traction a key part of your nursing care?

options.A: Anxious patients always disconnect their own traction
options.B: Good mental support replaces the need for pain meds
options.C: Stress stops bones from absorbing calcium
options.D: Being stuck in one position for weeks often brings down their mood and causes stress

explanation: Brilliant insight! Lying still for weeks takes a heavy emotional toll. Being a warm, listening ear is just as important as managing their physical injuries. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T7#GNS221_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the maximum safe weight typically applied during skin traction?

options.A: 10 to 15 kilograms
options.B: 4.5 to 5 kilograms
options.C: 30 to 35 kilograms
options.D: 20 to 25 kilograms

explanation: Heavier weights exceed the tensile strength of the skin and cause severe soft tissue damage instead of correcting bone alignment. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is skin traction considered a non-invasive orthopaedic procedure?

options.A: It involves no physical contact with the affected limb whatsoever
options.B: It relies entirely on internal fixation devices placed beneath the skin
options.C: It applies pulling force externally using tapes and boots without surgical pins
options.D: It requires minor surgical incisions to anchor the traction cords to muscles

explanation: Skin traction avoids breaking the bone or piercing the skin, using external devices like foam boots to distribute the pulling force. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h1)

question: A primary purpose of applying skin traction to a fractured femur is to achieve what outcome?

options.A: Reduce painful muscle spasms around the fracture site
options.B: Increase local blood circulation via heat generation
options.C: Promote rapid localized infection healing
options.D: Permanently fuse the broken bone ends together

explanation: The steady pulling force relaxes injured muscles, easing severe spasms that cause overlapping bone ends and intense pain. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h2)

question: Skin traction is most commonly used in clinical practice as which type of intervention?

options.A: A long-term outpatient rehabilitation exercise program
options.B: An emergency treatment for severe head injuries
options.C: A temporary measure before definitive surgical repair
options.D: A permanent substitute for open reduction internal fixation

explanation: Hospitals use skin traction to stabilize limbs while patients await surgery or until swelling subsides. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which traction type uses a foam boot and a straight longitudinal pull for lower limb injuries?

options.A: Balanced skeletal traction
options.B: Russell's traction
options.C: Buck's extension
options.D: Chin halter traction

explanation: Buck's extension applies a straight pull along the lower extremity using a boot to keep the leg immobilized. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the main difference between Buck's extension and Russell's traction?

options.A: Buck's extension requires a surgical pin drilled directly through the tibia
options.B: Russell's traction is used exclusively for upper arm fractures in children
options.C: Russell's traction adds a knee sling and pulley to allow knee movement
options.D: Buck's extension involves specialized weights suspended directly from the chin

explanation: Russell's traction incorporates a knee sling that supports the limb and permits controlled knee flexion during treatment. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h3)

question: What must the nurse do with traction weights during routine patient care shifts?

options.A: Ensure they hang freely without touching the floor or bed
options.B: Increase the weight daily to speed up bone healing
options.C: Rest them on the bed frame to give the patient a break
options.D: Remove them entirely during visiting hours to comfort family

explanation: Weights resting on any surface lose their tension, rendering the traction treatment completely ineffective. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why is patient counter-traction important in maintaining effective skin traction setups?

options.A: It allows the nurse to increase the traction weight beyond five kilograms
options.B: It eliminates the need to perform daily neurovascular assessments
options.C: It prevents the patient from sliding down and losing the pulling force
options.D: It ensures the weights touch the floor gently to reduce mechanical strain

explanation: Friction and body weight working in the opposite direction create the necessary counter-pull to keep the traction working properly. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT part of the standard 5 Ps neurovascular check?

options.A: Pulses
options.B: Peristalsis
options.C: Paralysis
options.D: Pallor

explanation: Peristalsis is a bowel function indicator, whereas the 5 Ps evaluate circulation, nerve function, and tissue perfusion in limbs. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h5)

question: A patient in skin traction reports sudden, severe pain that does not respond to prescribed analgesics. What does this finding suggest?

options.A: Standard skin irritation caused by the adhesive tape
options.B: Good tissue healing and successful bone alignment
options.C: Normal muscle relaxation indicating effective traction pull
options.D: Developing neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome

explanation: Unrelieved, escalating pain is often the earliest and most reliable warning sign of dangerously high pressure within the muscle compartment. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is a major risk specifically associated with the use of skin traction?

options.A: Skin breakdown and pressure ulcer formation
options.B: Permanent paralysis of the central nervous system
options.C: Systemic bone marrow suppression
options.D: Surgical site infection from bone pins

explanation: Constant pressure from boots and tapes against the skin easily compromises blood flow, leading to ulcers and blisters. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h6)

question: How should a nurse safely inspect the skin under skin traction straps?

options.A: Remove all weights and straps completely for two hours
options.B: Loosen one side at a time while supporting the limb
options.C: Cut away the traction tape using sharp surgical scissors
options.D: Apply antiseptic ointment directly over the adhesive tape

explanation: Inspecting one side at a time ensures the limb remains aligned and safe while allowing the nurse to check skin integrity underneath. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is an overhead trapeze bar particularly helpful for a patient in lower limb skin traction?

options.A: It allows the patient to lift their hips safely for bedpan use and pressure relief
options.B: It eliminates the risk of developing deep vein thrombosis in the legs
options.C: It completely replaces the need for daily neurovascular assessments
options.D: It serves as a mounting point to hang extra heavy traction weights

explanation: The trapeze bar enables upper body lifting, reducing shear forces on the skin when nursing staff provide bedpan care or skin checks. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h7)

question: A patient undergoing skin traction expresses deep frustration and anxiety over prolonged bed rest. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Acknowledge their feelings and explain the purpose and temporary nature of traction
options.B: Tell the patient that complaining will only delay their scheduled surgery
options.C: Request an immediate psychiatric evaluation for severe depression
options.D: Remove the traction weights immediately to let the patient walk around

explanation: Providing empathetic listening and clear rationale helps alleviate anxiety and fosters cooperation with the treatment plan. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T8#GNS221_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is the key difference between skeletal traction and skin traction?

options.A: Skin traction involves surgical insertion of metal wires
options.B: Skeletal traction attaches directly to the bone using pins
options.C: Skin traction uses heavy weights for longer periods
options.D: Skeletal traction only requires adhesive strips on the skin

explanation: You got this! Skeletal traction uses surgically placed pins to pull right on the bone, while skin traction applies the pulling force gently through the soft tissues outside. Great job! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why would a doctor choose skeletal traction over skin traction for a broken femur?

options.A: It requires no special monitoring by nursing staff
options.B: It completely eliminates the risk of infection
options.C: It allows much heavier weights to be used safely
options.D: It permits the patient to walk around the ward freely

explanation: Spot on! Because the pull goes straight to the bone, skeletal traction can handle the heavy weights needed to realign a big bone like the femur without tearing the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h1)

question: As a nurse, what must you always check regarding the weights in a skeletal traction setup?

options.A: Remove them every four hours to rest the leg
options.B: Rest them on the bed frame when turning the patient
options.C: Increase the weight daily to speed up healing
options.D: Ensure they hang freely without touching the floor

explanation: Well done! The weights must always hang completely free so the right amount of pulling force stays constant on the bone. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the main job of counter-traction in a skeletal traction setup?

options.A: To double the amount of pulling force on the bone
options.B: To prevent the patient from sliding down and altering the pull
options.C: To keep the ropes from slipping out of the pulley grooves
options.D: To eliminate the need for regular pin site cleaning

explanation: Exactly! Counter-traction uses the patient's own body weight and gravity to pull in the opposite direction, keeping the traction steady and effective. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h2)

question: What are the core checks to perform during a neurovascular assessment of a limb in traction?

options.A: Joint range, breath sounds, and pulses
options.B: Pain scale, pin length, and skin turgor
options.C: Circulation, motion, and sensation
options.D: Temperature, weight, and muscle tone

explanation: You nailed it! Always remember the ABCs of neurovascular checks: checking if blood is flowing (circulation), if they can move (motion), and if they can feel (sensation). [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h3)

question: A patient in skeletal traction suddenly complains of severe pain and numb toes in the affected leg. What should you do first?

options.A: Check the equipment alignment and notify the physician immediately
options.B: Increase the hanging weight to relieve pressure
options.C: Give a sleeping pill and turn the patient on their side
options.D: Remove the skeletal traction pin at the bedside

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Sudden pain and numbness mean blood flow or nerves might be squeezed. Always check the setup first and call the doctor right away. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the biggest risk you watch out for at skeletal traction pin sites?

options.A: Development of bone infection like osteomyelitis
options.B: Rapid healing that fuses the pin to the bed sheets
options.C: Complete numbness of the entire unaffected leg
options.D: Permanent discoloration of the surrounding skin

explanation: Spot on! Because the pins go right through the skin, bacteria can travel down the metal and cause a serious bone infection. Good thing nurses keep a close eye on this! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h4)

question: Which finding around a skeletal traction pin site should you report as a sign of infection?

options.A: Purulent drainage and foul odor
options.B: Dry crusting around the metal insertion point
options.C: Mild pinkness that fades within the first day
options.D: Small amounts of clear serosanguinous drainage

explanation: You got it! Pus and bad smells are telltale signs of bacteria at work. Light pinkness or dry crusting can just be normal early healing. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h4)

question: Which lung issue is most common for a patient stuck on prolonged bed rest in traction?

options.A: Hyperventilation syndrome
options.B: Asthma attack
options.C: Atelectasis
options.D: Spontaneous pneumothorax

explanation: Well done! Lying flat and breathing shallowly can cause small air sacs in the lungs to collapse (atelectasis). That's why deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry are so important! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why are sequential compression devices (SCDs) often used for patients in skeletal traction?

options.A: To reduce swelling by pushing fluid into the weights
options.B: To prevent deep vein thrombosis from immobility
options.C: To stimulate muscle growth while the bone heals
options.D: To anchor the patient's leg so the rope stays taut

explanation: Spot on! Staying still slows down blood flow in the legs, putting patients at risk for blood clots (DVT). SCDs gently squeeze the legs to keep the blood moving nicely. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h5)

question: When is skeletal traction usually taken off?

options.A: When the patient is ready for surgery, casting, or healing allows
options.B: As soon as the patient gets bored on bed rest
options.C: When the pin site develops normal crusting
options.D: Exactly 24 hours after the pin was put in

explanation: You got it! Skeletal traction is a temporary helper. It comes off once definitive care like surgery or a cast takes over, or when the bone is stable enough. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is your main priority as a nurse right after skeletal traction is removed?

options.A: Supporting the limb carefully to prevent sudden pain or injury
options.B: Removing the patient's compression stockings and bed rest orders
options.C: Discharging the patient home immediately
options.D: Scrubbing the old pin sites with strong iodine to remove all scars

explanation: Brilliant! Once the traction is gone, the limb is unsupported and vulnerable. Always handle the limb with extra care to keep the patient safe and comfortable. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T9#GNS221_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of performing a neurological examination?

options.A: To determine the exact blood type of the patient
options.B: To measure the patient's daily caloric intake
options.C: To diagnose specific psychiatric disorders
options.D: To evaluate the function of the nervous system

explanation: The neurological exam is specifically designed to assess how well the central and peripheral nervous systems are working. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is establishing a baseline neurological assessment important for a patient?

options.A: It eliminates the need for vital sign monitoring
options.B: It gives a starting point to track future changes in status
options.C: It completely prevents any future neurological complications
options.D: It determines the patient's exact date of hospital discharge

explanation: Having a clear baseline allows the healthcare team to notice early signs of improvement or deterioration. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why should a nurse explain neurological tests using simple, non-medical terms?

options.A: To shorten the overall duration of the hospital stay
options.B: To reduce patient anxiety and improve cooperation
options.C: To replace the need for a physical examination
options.D: To avoid documenting the assessment in the medical record

explanation: Clear and simple communication helps calm the patient so they can participate fully and accurately in the assessment. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h2)

question: Your patient looks nervous while you get ready to test their cranial nerves. What should you do first?

options.A: Proceed quickly with the exam to get it finished
options.B: Skip the neurological assessment entirely for the day
options.C: Administer a strong sedative medication immediately
options.D: Explain each step simply before performing it

explanation: Well done! Addressing your patient's worry with a gentle explanation builds trust and makes them feel much more comfortable. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which piece of equipment is primarily used to elicit deep tendon reflexes during a neurological exam?

options.A: Reflex hammer
options.B: Penlight
options.C: Ophthalmoscope
options.D: Tongue depressor

explanation: A reflex hammer is the standard tool used to gently tap tendons and assess spinal reflex arcs. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why is a quiet environment important when conducting a neurological assessment?

options.A: To prevent the hospital equipment from malfunctioning
options.B: To keep the patient fast asleep throughout the examination
options.C: To ensure the lighting remains perfectly dim at all times
options.D: To accurately evaluate mental status, speech, and cranial nerves

explanation: Excessive background noise can distract the patient or mask subtle speech and hearing abnormalities. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h3)

question: How many major components typically make up a comprehensive neurological assessment?

options.A: Eight
options.B: Twelve
options.C: Two
options.D: Five

explanation: The standard exam covers mental status, cranial nerves, motor system, sensory system, and reflexes. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is evaluated when assessing the sensory system during a neurological exam?

options.A: Light touch and pain perception
options.B: Muscle bulk and involuntary twitching
options.C: Deep tendon reflex hammer response
options.D: Level of orientation to time and place

explanation: Sensory evaluations focus on how well the patient perceives external stimuli like touch, pain, and vibration. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h4)

question: When does the assessment of a patient's mental status actually begin?

options.A: Only after the deep tendon reflexes are completed
options.B: The moment you first greet and observe the patient
options.C: After the patient falls asleep for the night
options.D: When the laboratory blood work results return

explanation: Observation of appearance, alertness, and interaction starts immediately upon entering the room. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h5)

question: What does asking a patient to smile and puff out their cheeks help evaluate?

options.A: Cranial nerve I
options.B: Cranial nerve II
options.C: Cranial nerve VII
options.D: Cranial nerve VIII

explanation: Cranial nerve VII is the facial nerve, which controls facial expressions and movement. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why should a patient close their eyes during sensory testing?

options.A: To protect their eyes from bright overhead hospital lights
options.B: To prevent them from using visual cues to guide their answers
options.C: To prevent dizziness caused by looking around the room
options.D: To help them fall asleep during a lengthy examination

explanation: Closing the eyes ensures that the patient is genuinely feeling the stimulus rather than just watching where you touch. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h6)

question: When assessing muscle strength, how should the nurse evaluate the limbs?

options.A: By measuring the exact circumference with a tape
options.B: Bilaterally to compare both sides of the body
options.C: Only after administering pain medication
options.D: Only on the dominant side to save time

explanation: Comparing opposite sides helps identify localized weakness or asymmetry caused by neurological injury. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which tool is most commonly used for rapid neurological assessment in emergency settings?

options.A: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.B: Comprehensive mental status questionnaire
options.C: Deep tendon reflex chart
options.D: Full cranial nerve checklist

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale provides a quick, reliable score for eye, verbal, and motor responses during emergencies. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the best way to assess a toddler's neurological function during a physical exam?

options.A: Observe their spontaneous play and developmental milestones
options.B: Ask them to complete a written multiple-choice test
options.C: Keep them completely still and silent for thirty minutes
options.D: Perform a strict formal cranial nerve exam immediately

explanation: Toddlers cannot follow complex commands, so observing natural movement and play provides the best clinical insight. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why should you avoid writing vague words like 'normal' when charting a neurological exam?

options.A: It is illegal to use descriptive words in hospital charts
options.B: It prevents doctors from ordering blood laboratory tests
options.C: It automatically delays the patient's discharge process
options.D: It does not provide specific baseline data for future comparison

explanation: Spot on! Clear measurements and detailed descriptions help other nurses track exact changes over time. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h8)

question: You finish a neuro check and notice a brand new weakness in your patient's right arm. What should you do right away?

options.A: Discharge the patient home with instructions to rest
options.B: Wait until the end of your shift to write it in the chart
options.C: Report the finding immediately to the healthcare provider
options.D: Assume the patient is just tired and ignore the finding

explanation: You made the right call! Sudden neurological changes always need quick medical attention to keep your patient safe. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h8)

question: What is the main reason doctors perform a liver biopsy?

options.A: To take a tiny tissue sample to check under a microscope
options.B: To drain excess fluid from the belly
options.C: To flush out toxins from the bile ducts
options.D: To check the blood pressure inside the liver

explanation: Spot on! A liver biopsy is simply taking a tiny piece of liver tissue so the lab can look at the cells and figure out what's going on. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h1)

question: When is a doctor most likely to order a liver biopsy?

options.A: For routine check-ups on healthy students
options.B: To check how well the kidneys are filtering waste
options.C: When blood tests and scans don't explain strange liver results
options.D: When a patient is just feeling tired and slightly dehydrated

explanation: You got it! When basic tests like blood work and ultrasounds leave doctors guessing, a biopsy helps give a clear, definitive answer. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why would a bleeding disorder make a liver biopsy unsafe?

options.A: It can cause temporary muscle stiffness
options.B: It stops the kidneys from working properly
options.C: The liver has so many blood vessels, risking severe internal bleeding
options.D: It can cause a sudden skin infection

explanation: Correct! Because the liver is packed with blood vessels, a patient who cannot clot well is at high risk for dangerous internal bleeding. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why is severe fluid in the abdomen (ascites) a big risk during a liver biopsy?

options.A: It destroys all clotting factors in the blood
options.B: It makes the liver float around, making it hard to hit the target with the needle
options.C: It stops numbing medicine from working on the skin
options.D: It makes the patient stop breathing entirely

explanation: That's right! Too much fluid makes the liver shift position, meaning the needle might miss the spot or accidentally poke something else. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h2)

question: As a nurse, what is a crucial check to make *before* a patient goes for a liver biopsy?

options.A: Check that clotting blood tests are safe and consent is signed
options.B: Perform a minor surgery to drain belly fluid
options.C: Give them strong general anesthesia right in the ward
options.D: Make sure they eat a large heavy meal

explanation: Spot on! Safety first—always verify clotting labs and make sure the patient understands and signs the consent form before the procedure. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h3)

question: Your patient scheduled for a liver biopsy says they just took their morning dose of warfarin (a blood thinner). What should you do?

options.A: Tell them to walk around the ward to sweat it out
options.B: Go ahead with the test since morning doses do not matter
options.C: Inform the doctor immediately and expect the test to be delayed
options.D: Give them vitamin K right away to reverse it

explanation: You nailed it. Warfarin thins the blood and raises bleeding risks, so the doctor must be told right away so they can reschedule safely. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h3)

question: How should a patient lie during a standard percutaneous liver biopsy?

options.A: On their left side with knees pulled up
options.B: Flat on their back with their right hand placed behind their head
options.C: Sitting upright leaning over a bedside table
options.D: Flat on their stomach with arms stretched forward

explanation: Great job! This position opens up the right side of the chest wall, giving the doctor the best access to the liver. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why is the patient told to hold their breath while the doctor inserts the needle?

options.A: To stop air from entering through the skin
options.B: To keep their blood pressure from dropping too low
options.C: To keep the diaphragm still so the liver doesn't get torn
options.D: To save oxygen in case they feel stressed

explanation: Correct! Holding the breath stops the chest and diaphragm from moving, keeping the liver completely still for a safe, clean needle entry. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h4)

question: What position is best for a patient immediately *after* a liver biopsy?

options.A: On their right side with a pillow pressing against the biopsy site
options.B: Flat on their back with legs raised high
options.C: Sitting straight up at a 90-degree angle
options.D: On their left side with knees tucked

explanation: You got it! Lying on the right side puts gentle pressure right where the needle went in, helping to prevent bleeding. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h5)

question: What are the earliest vital sign clues that a patient might be bleeding internally after a biopsy?

options.A: Sudden high blood pressure and a very slow pulse
options.B: Falling blood pressure and a fast heart rate
options.C: Rising fever and flushed skin
options.D: Slow, deep breathing with high oxygen levels

explanation: Spot on! When blood is lost inside, blood volume drops. The heart beats faster to make up for it, while blood pressure starts to slide down. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why might a patient complain of right shoulder pain after a liver biopsy?

options.A: Muscle strain from keeping their hand behind their head
options.B: Mild irritation traveling down from the bladder
options.C: A nearby nerve (the phrenic nerve) gets slightly irritated, causing referred pain
options.D: The nurse pulled their arm too hard during positioning

explanation: Correct! The phrenic nerve shares pathways with the liver area, so irritation near the liver can trick the brain into feeling pain up in the right shoulder. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which sign might tell you a patient has developed a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) after a liver biopsy?

options.A: Inability to control their bladder
options.B: Sudden trouble breathing and reduced breath sounds on the right side
options.C: Yellow skin and eyes appearing within an hour
options.D: Painful bruising right on the skin puncture site

explanation: You nailed it! Since the liver sits right under the lung, a misplaced needle can let air into the chest cavity, leading to breathing trouble on that side. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h6)

question: What activity rule should you teach a patient before they go home after a liver biopsy?

options.A: Eat no solid foods for the next five days
options.B: Avoid heavy lifting and hard exercise for at least a week
options.C: Stay in bed in a dark room for two whole weeks
options.D: Keep your right arm strapped in a sling for two days

explanation: Spot on! Straining or lifting increases pressure inside the belly, which can trigger bleeding even days later. Rest is key! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h7)

question: Which home care instruction is most critical for a patient who just had a liver biopsy?

options.A: Call the clinic or return if you feel severe shoulder or belly pain
options.B: Go for long daily jogs to boost blood circulation
options.C: Scrub the tiny wound hard with soap immediately
options.D: Take aspirin every morning to prevent clots

explanation: You got it! Severe pain can be an early warning sign of internal bleeding or other complications, so patients must report it right away. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T10#GNS221_U2_T10_h7)

question: What do standard Liver Function Tests (LFTs) primarily check in the blood?

options.A: Red blood cell count and hemoglobin levels
options.B: Enzymes and proteins related to the liver
options.C: Electrolytes and kidney filtration rates
options.D: Clotting factors only produced in the bone marrow

explanation: You've got this! LFTs simply look at substances made, processed, or released by the liver to see how well it's doing its job. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why can it be a bit misleading to call every test in an LFT panel a 'function' test?

options.A: They can only be performed after a surgical liver biopsy
options.B: Some markers measure cell damage rather than actual working capacity
options.C: They measure waste products filtered exclusively by the kidneys
options.D: They only measure the gallbladder and not the liver tissue

explanation: Great thinking! Tests like transaminases actually show us if liver cells are injured or leaking, rather than directly measuring how much work the liver can do. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which liver enzyme is known to be more specific to liver cell injury?

options.A: AST
options.B: Amylase
options.C: ALT
options.D: Lipase

explanation: Spot on! Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is concentrated mostly inside liver cells, making it a reliable red flag when liver tissue is damaged. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h2)

question: A patient comes in with a suspected paracetamol overdose. Which LFT enzyme results will you expect to shoot up first?

options.A: Albumin and total protein
options.B: ALT and AST
options.C: Amylase and lipase
options.D: Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine

explanation: Well done! Too much paracetamol causes sudden injury to liver cells, spilling intracellular enzymes like ALT and AST quickly into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the main reason a patient's serum bilirubin level shoots up?

options.A: Low dietary intake of essential amino acids
options.B: Excessive production of red blood cells in the kidneys
options.C: Impaired liver processing or bile duct blockage
options.D: Dehydration from severe vomiting and diarrhea

explanation: Exactly! Bilirubin builds up in the blood when the liver is struggling to process it or when something is blocking the bile passages. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h3)

question: Why is a low blood albumin level usually a sign of long-standing (chronic) liver trouble rather than a sudden issue?

options.A: Albumin is stored in large amounts in fat tissue before being released
options.B: Acute liver injury causes albumin to temporarily hide inside the kidneys
options.C: Albumin has a long half-life, so levels drop slowly over weeks of poor production
options.D: The body stops producing red blood cells before it stops making albumin

explanation: You're getting the hang of this! Because albumin stays in circulation for about three weeks, it takes a while of poor liver production for levels to noticeably crash. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which clinical sign will immediately make a doctor or nurse think of ordering a liver function panel?

options.A: Frequent coughing
options.B: Painful urination
options.C: Jaundice
options.D: Swollen ankles from heart failure

explanation: Spot on! That yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice) tells us bilirubin isn't clearing properly, making LFTs a top priority. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h4)

question: What does a high Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) level mostly point toward?

options.A: Severe acute viral hepatitis infection
options.B: Chronic kidney filtration failure
options.C: Bile duct obstruction or bone activity
options.D: Massive breakdown of red blood cells

explanation: Brilliant! ALP hangs out in the bile ducts and bones, so high numbers usually point your clinical suspicion toward biliary issues or bone growth/turnover. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h4)

question: Why do you need to watch the needle site extra carefully after drawing blood from someone with severe liver disease?

options.A: Their veins are usually completely collapsed from chronic fluid overload
options.B: Their skin is too fragile to tolerate standard adhesive tape
options.C: They often have poor clotting due to low production of clotting factors
options.D: Local anesthetics used during the draw can cause severe allergic reactions

explanation: You nailed it! A struggling liver can't pump out enough clotting proteins, meaning your patient is at a higher risk of prolonged bleeding or bruising after a needle stick. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which of these tasks is NOT part of a nurse's daily responsibilities when dealing with LFTs?

options.A: Monitoring the blood draw site for bleeding afterward
options.B: Diagnosing the specific stage of cirrhosis from the lab slip
options.C: Ensuring proper patient preparation and fasting if required
options.D: Checking patient medication history for drugs that stress the liver

explanation: That's right! We prep the patient, check medications, and keep them safe, but making the final disease diagnosis is the doctor's job. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T11#GNS221_U2_T11_h5)

question: What does a fasting blood sugar test primarily measure?

options.A: Baseline blood glucose after food restriction
options.B: Maximum blood glucose right after a heavy meal
options.C: Average blood sugar over the last three months
options.D: Total amount of insulin stored in the pancreas

explanation: The test measures glucose levels when the body has not consumed calories for several hours, showing the true resting baseline. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is it important to test blood sugar while a patient is fasting?

options.A: It makes the red blood cells easier to see under a microscope.
options.B: It forces the pancreas to release all remaining insulin stores.
options.C: It prevents the patient from feeling dizzy during the blood draw.
options.D: It removes the temporary glucose spikes caused by recent eating.

explanation: Food intake naturally raises blood sugar temporarily, so fasting gives a clear baseline without dietary interference. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which pancreatic hormone lowers blood sugar by helping cells take in glucose?

options.A: Glucagon
options.B: Cortisol
options.C: Adrenaline
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Insulin acts as the primary hormone that allows body cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream, thereby lowering blood sugar. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the primary role of glucagon during a fasting state?

options.A: To signal the liver to release stored glucose into the blood
options.B: To help the pancreas produce more beta cells for energy
options.C: To block insulin from entering the muscle tissues
options.D: To transport excess sugar directly to the kidneys for excretion

explanation: When fasting lowers blood sugar, glucagon tells the liver to break down stored glycogen to keep blood sugar from dropping too low. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which symptom is a classic indicator that prompts a doctor to order a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: Sudden low blood pressure and dizziness
options.B: Excessive thirst and frequent urination
options.C: Swelling in the lower legs and ankles
options.D: Yellowing of the skin and eyes

explanation: Polydipsia and polyuria are hallmark signs of high blood sugar that signal the need for diagnostic screening. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h3)

question: A healthy pregnant woman at 26 weeks gestation goes for her routine antenatal clinic. Why is a glucose screening typically included?

options.A: To check for gestational diabetes that can develop during pregnancy
options.B: To confirm the exact gestational age of the growing fetus
options.C: To test her kidney function against pregnancy hormones
options.D: To measure how much iron she is storing in her liver

explanation: Pregnancy hormones can cause insulin resistance, making routine screening for gestational diabetes essential during the second trimester. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h3)

question: What is the minimum recommended fasting time before a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: 24 hours
options.B: 4 hours
options.C: 8 hours
options.D: 2 hours

explanation: A minimum of 8 hours without caloric intake is required to ensure the digestive system is at rest and baseline glucose can be measured. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h4)

question: Which beverage is generally allowed during the fasting period prior to the test?

options.A: Black coffee
options.B: Fruit juice
options.C: Plain water
options.D: Sweetened tea

explanation: Plain water has no calories or active compounds that stimulate digestion, keeping the fasting state intact while preventing dehydration. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h4)

question: What special chemical is added to the blood collection tube for a fasting blood sugar test to keep the blood cells from eating up the sugar?

options.A: Potassium EDTA
options.B: Sodium fluoride
options.C: Heparin sulfate
options.D: Calcium chloride

explanation: Great job! Sodium fluoride acts as a preservative (glycolytic inhibitor) that stops red blood cells from consuming the glucose in the tube before the lab technician can test it. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h5)

question: When should the nurse label the collected blood specimen tube?

options.A: At the bedside immediately after the blood draw
options.B: Inside the laboratory before handing it to the technician
options.C: At the nursing station after finishing all morning rounds
options.D: Before entering the patient room to save time

explanation: Labeling specimens at the bedside immediately after collection ensures proper patient identification and prevents mislabeling errors. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h5)

question: What is the standard normal fasting blood sugar range for a healthy adult?

options.A: Below 100 mg/dL
options.B: 140 to 180 mg/dL
options.C: 200 to 250 mg/dL
options.D: Above 300 mg/dL

explanation: A fasting blood sugar reading under 100 mg/dL is considered normal for individuals without metabolic disorders. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h6)

question: A patient's fasting blood sugar result comes back at 115 mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: It is completely normal and requires no further follow-up.
options.B: It indicates prediabetes or impaired fasting glucose.
options.C: It confirms that the patient has full-blown Type 1 diabetes.
options.D: It shows severe hypoglycemia requiring immediate sugar intake.

explanation: Values between 100 and 125 mg/dL fall into the prediabetes range, signaling a need for lifestyle changes. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h6)

question: What term is used to describe a dangerously low fasting blood sugar level?

options.A: Hypoglycemia
options.B: Hemoconcentration
options.C: Glycosuria
options.D: Hyperglycemia

explanation: Hypoglycemia refers to blood glucose levels falling below the normal healthy threshold, typically under 70 mg/dL. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h7)

question: A patient with diabetes has a fasting blood sugar of 55 mg/dL and is shaky and confused. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?

options.A: Kidney failure causing a backup of metabolic waste
options.B: A normal reaction to an overnight fasting period
options.C: Dehydration from drinking too much plain water
options.D: Brain glucose deprivation from low blood sugar

explanation: When blood sugar drops too low, the brain lacks energy, causing neurological symptoms like confusion and shaking. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why can severe physical stress or a sudden infection cause a high fasting blood sugar reading?

options.A: Infection causes the kidneys to stop filtering sugar out of the blood.
options.B: Dehydration turns blood cells into pure glucose molecules.
options.C: Fever completely destroys insulin molecules stored in the pancreas.
options.D: Stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline are released, raising blood glucose.

explanation: You've got this! Acute stress triggers your body to release hormones that push stored glucose into the bloodstream to give you energy for a fight-or-flight response. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h8)

question: Which medication class is well known for increasing blood sugar levels during therapy?

options.A: Laxatives
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Antihistamines

explanation: Corticosteroids stimulate hepatic glucose production and induce insulin resistance, frequently raising blood sugar levels. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h8)

question: What is the most important immediate nursing action after a fasting blood draw for a patient with diabetes?

options.A: Provide food and allow the patient to take held morning medications.
options.B: Send the patient home immediately without checking the puncture site.
options.C: Instruct the patient to continue fasting until the lab results return.
options.D: Encourage the patient to run on a treadmill to lower blood sugar.

explanation: Well done! Because the patient fasted and held their morning diabetes drugs, they need food and their routine medications right away to prevent their blood sugar from crashing. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h9)

question: What key lifestyle advice should a nurse include when educating a patient with prediabetes?

options.A: Avoid all types of physical movement to preserve energy
options.B: Sleep for at least fourteen hours every single night
options.C: Incorporate a balanced diet and regular physical activity
options.D: Eliminate all forms of water from the daily diet

explanation: Dietary changes and regular exercise help improve insulin sensitivity and prevent prediabetes from advancing to full diabetes. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h9)

question: What is the primary substance used as a contrast medium during a barium swallow procedure?

options.A: Barium sulfate
options.B: Gadolinium chelate
options.C: Iodinated contrast
options.D: Normal saline

explanation: Barium sulfate is a dense, radiopaque compound that coats the lining of the digestive tract, allowing it to show up clearly on X-ray imaging. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why is fluoroscopy a key component of a barium swallow test?

options.A: It provides real-time moving images of swallowing and peristalsis
options.B: It permanently removes small blockages in the throat
options.C: It measures the exact pH levels inside the stomach
options.D: It checks the patient's blood pressure throughout the scan

explanation: Unlike standard still X-rays, fluoroscopy acts like an X-ray movie, letting the radiologist watch how food and liquid move down the throat in real time. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h1)

question: What is the most critical absolute contraindication for a standard barium swallow test?

options.A: Controlled type 2 diabetes
options.B: Suspected gastrointestinal perforation
options.C: A history of seasonal allergies
options.D: Mild chronic hypertension

explanation: If barium leaks outside a torn or perforated gut wall into the body cavities, it causes a severe, dangerous inflammatory reaction. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h2)

question: A patient with severe swallowing difficulties and chronic heartburn is scheduled for an upper GI diagnostic test. Which condition would make you question an order for a standard barium swallow?

options.A: A suspected tear in the wall of the esophagus
options.B: A past history of childhood asthma
options.C: A reported fear of small enclosed spaces
options.D: Mild discomfort after eating heavy meals

explanation: A suspected tear means perforation is possible, which completely rules out barium due to the risk of severe tissue damage from leaked contrast. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h2)

question: How long must a patient typically fast (NPO) before a barium swallow examination?

options.A: 30 minutes
options.B: No fasting is needed
options.C: 6 to 8 hours
options.D: 24 full hours

explanation: An empty stomach is required so that food residue does not block the view of the mucosal lining or mimic a tumor on the X-ray. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why are patients advised not to smoke on the morning of their barium swallow test?

options.A: Smoking causes immediate closure of the upper esophageal sphincter
options.B: Smoking increases stomach acid and swallowing secretions
options.C: Nicotine dissolves the barium contrast inside the mouth
options.D: The X-ray machine reacts poorly with tobacco smoke in the room

explanation: Nicotine stimulates gastric activity and excess saliva or acid production, which can interfere with clear imaging of the upper GI tract. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of tilting the X-ray table into different angles during a barium swallow?

options.A: To drain excess stomach fluids before the contrast is given
options.B: To help gravity coat the entire lining of the esophagus and stomach with barium
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling asleep during the procedure
options.D: To speed up the digestion of the barium into the bloodstream

explanation: Changing table positions ensures that the liquid barium flows over all mucosal surfaces so small defects or ulcers are not missed. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is the approximate time it takes to complete a standard barium swallow procedure?

options.A: Exactly 5 minutes
options.B: 2 to 3 hours
options.C: Over 24 hours
options.D: 15 to 30 minutes

explanation: Most standard barium swallow exams are relatively quick, taking between a quarter to half an hour depending on patient cooperation and findings. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h4)

question: How should the normal esophagus appear on a healthy barium swallow image?

options.A: A wide pouch with multiple jagged blockages
options.B: A rigid, non-moving tube with thickened walls
options.C: A smooth, straight tubular structure with uniform width
options.D: A completely closed channel with zero contrast entry

explanation: A healthy esophagus shows an even, smooth column of barium moving down without unusual narrowing, widening, or pouching. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h5)

question: What does the presence of normal peristaltic stripping waves indicate in the esophagus?

options.A: An abnormal blockage trapping fluid inside the upper chest
options.B: A complete failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax
options.C: The presence of a large sliding hiatal hernia in the hiatus
options.D: Coordinated muscle contractions pushing food and contrast downward

explanation: Peristaltic waves are the rhythmic muscular squeezes of the esophagus that successfully clear the barium bolus into the stomach. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h5)

question: Which condition is classically associated with a "bird-beak" tapering appearance at the bottom of the esophagus?

options.A: Zenker's diverticulum
options.B: Hiatal hernia
options.C: Gastric ulcer
options.D: Achalasia

explanation: Achalasia prevents the lower esophageal sphincter from opening properly, creating a narrow, bird-beak shape on the X-ray film as barium tries to pass. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h6)

question: A patient's barium swallow report mentions a pouch-like herniation of the mucosal wall in the upper throat area. Which condition matches this description?

options.A: Gastroesophageal reflux
options.B: Esophageal carcinoma
options.C: Sliding hiatal hernia
options.D: Zenker's diverticulum

explanation: A Zenker's diverticulum is an outpouching that occurs in the pharyngoesophageal junction, trapping food particles and causing regurgitation. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h6)

question: What color should the nurse tell the patient their stool might appear for a few days after a barium swallow?

options.A: Bright red or bloody
options.B: Jet black and tarry
options.C: Neon green or yellow
options.D: Chalky white or light gray

explanation: The elimination of residual unabsorbed barium sulfate naturally turns the stool a pale, chalky white or gray color until it is completely cleared. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h7)

question: A patient who had a barium swallow two days ago reports no bowel movement, abdominal cramping, and bloating. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Immediate healing of an esophageal ulcer
options.B: A normal reaction to fasting before the test
options.C: Rapid absorption of contrast into the blood
options.D: Barium impaction leading to constipation

explanation: Barium dries out inside the large intestine, making constipation and impaction a major post-procedure risk if fluids and laxatives are not used. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h7)

question: Why is encouraging increased fluid intake the most crucial home care instruction after a barium swallow?

options.A: To dilute any remaining stomach acid and prevent heartburn symptoms
options.B: To speed up the healing of small tears made during the X-ray
options.C: To prevent the barium from hardening and causing constipation or bowel blockage
options.D: To help the kidneys absorb the radioactive barium into the urine

explanation: Extra fluids keep the barium mixture moving smoothly through the colon, preventing it from turning into a concrete-like blockage. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h8)

question: Which post-procedure symptom should a patient report to the healthcare provider immediately?

options.A: A mild chalky taste remaining in the mouth briefly
options.B: Passing pale white stools for the first 24 hours
options.C: Feeling slightly tired after changing positions on the table
options.D: Severe abdominal pain and inability to pass gas

explanation: Severe abdominal pain and lack of gas or stool suggest a bowel obstruction from hardened barium, which requires urgent medical attention. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h8)

question: Why do we use barium sulfate during a barium meal X-ray test?

options.A: To act as a contrast medium on X-rays
options.B: To neutralize excess stomach acid
options.C: To numb the lining of the stomach
options.D: To speed up the digestion of food

explanation: You're doing great! Barium coats the inside of the gut and blocks X-rays so we can see the organs clearly on the screen. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which parts of the body do we primarily look at during a standard barium meal test?

options.A: Esophagus, stomach, and duodenum
options.B: Ascending and descending colon
options.C: Jejunum, ileum, and cecum
options.D: Liver, gallbladder, and pancreas

explanation: Spot on! A barium meal focuses specifically on the upper digestive tract, from your throat down to the upper part of the small intestine. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h1)

question: When a patient has 'dysphagia', what exact trouble are they experiencing?

options.A: Frequent vomiting
options.B: Severe stomach pain
options.C: Involuntary weight loss
options.D: Difficulty swallowing

explanation: You've got this! Dysphagia is just the medical word for trouble or pain when swallowing food or drinks. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h2)

question: A patient comes in with burning upper tummy pain, and the doctor suspects a stomach ulcer. Which test is the doctor most likely to order first?

options.A: A lower GI series
options.B: A barium meal
options.C: A pelvic ultrasound
options.D: An intravenous pyelogram

explanation: Well done! A barium meal is great for showing the inner lining of the stomach and duodenum so we can spot ulcers easily. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h2)

question: Why is a suspected hole (perforation) in the gut a major warning sign against using regular barium?

options.A: The X-ray machine cannot see through leaked barium
options.B: Barium leaks into the abdomen and causes severe inflammation
options.C: The barium will instantly dissolve in the bloodstream
options.D: It will cause immediate kidney failure

explanation: Think of it this way: if the gut has a hole, barium can leak out into the belly and cause a very dangerous reaction and infection. Safety first! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h3)

question: If a doctor suspects a hole in the patient's gut, what type of contrast dye is used instead of barium?

options.A: Thick barium paste
options.B: Water-soluble contrast
options.C: Oily contrast dye
options.D: Air contrast only

explanation: Brilliant! Water-soluble dyes are much safer because if they leak out, the body can easily absorb them without causing a major crisis. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h3)

question: How many hours should a patient normally fast before doing a barium meal test?

options.A: Exactly 30 minutes
options.B: 6 to 8 hours
options.C: 24 to 36 hours
options.D: 1 to 2 hours

explanation: You're doing great! An empty stomach for 6 to 8 hours ensures leftover food won't hide tiny ulcers or tumors on the X-ray. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h4)

question: As a nurse, why would you advise a patient not to smoke on the morning of their barium meal test?

options.A: Smoking increases stomach acid and gut movement
options.B: Nicotine stains the inside of the X-ray machine
options.C: Smoking causes the barium mixture to curdle
options.D: Nicotine interferes with the water-soluble dye

explanation: Spot on! Nicotine wakes up the stomach, making extra juices and movements that can blur the pictures we need. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h4)

question: What special X-ray technology does the radiologist use to watch the barium move in real-time?

options.A: Thermography
options.B: Electrocardiography
options.C: Fluoroscopy
options.D: Magnetic resonance

explanation: Keep it up! Fluoroscopy is basically an X-ray movie, letting the doctor watch the drink flow through your system live. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why do they sometimes give patients gas-producing crystals along with the barium?

options.A: To numb the throat during swallowing
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nauseated by the barium
options.C: To speed up the emptying of the stomach contents
options.D: To provide a double-contrast view of the stomach lining

explanation: Brilliant! The gas blows the stomach open like a balloon, pressing the barium against the walls so we get super-clear pictures. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h5)

question: What color should a nurse expect the patient's stool to be for the first couple of days after a barium meal?

options.A: Bright red or bloody
options.B: Jet black and tarry
options.C: Chalky white or pale gray
options.D: Dark green and watery

explanation: You're doing fantastic! Since barium is a heavy white mineral, it turns the poo a distinct pale or chalky color as it leaves the body. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h6)

question: Why must we encourage patients to drink plenty of water right after a barium meal?

options.A: To prevent the patient from developing a high fever
options.B: To prevent severe constipation caused by the barium
options.C: To dissolve any leftover barium remaining in the stomach
options.D: To speed up the absorption of the contrast into the blood

explanation: Spot on! Barium soaks up water like a sponge as it moves down, so extra fluids save your patient from a hard, painful time in the toilet. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the most common side effect patients experience after a barium meal test?

options.A: Severe hair loss
options.B: Kidney failure
options.C: Internal bleeding
options.D: Constipation

explanation: You've got this! Because barium dries things out inside the bowel, constipation is the number one thing to watch out for afterward. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which group of patients is at the highest risk of accidentally breathing in (aspirating) barium during the test?

options.A: Patients with a history of high blood pressure
options.B: Patients with severe swallowing difficulties
options.C: Patients who receive a mild laxative post-test
options.D: Patients who fasted for longer than twelve hours

explanation: Good clinical thinking! If someone already struggles to swallow, they can easily choke and pull the barium down into their lungs. Always assess carefully! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h7)

question: What is the main goal of performing a vulvar swab?

options.A: To measure the internal pH of the vaginal canal accurately
options.B: To collect microbial samples from the external female genitalia
options.C: To empty residual fluid from the urinary bladder completely
options.D: To remove excess tissue growth from the labia minora safely

explanation: You've got this! A vulvar swab is simply used to collect samples from the outside parts to find out what germ is causing issues like itching or unusual discharge. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h1)

question: Why must you know the anatomy of the vulva well before taking a sample?

options.A: To determine the exact hormonal cycle day of the patient accurately
options.B: To calculate the correct dosage of antibiotics needed for treatment
options.C: To prevent the patient from feeling any discomfort during the procedure
options.D: To ensure the sample is collected from the exact symptomatic area

explanation: Knowing your landmarks—like the labia and clitoris—helps you swab the exact spot where the sore or discharge is, ensuring accurate lab results! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which patient position is standard for a vulvar swab?

options.A: Lateral recovery position
options.B: Prone flat position
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Dorsal lithotomy position

explanation: The dorsal lithotomy position (lying on the back with legs supported) gives you the best view and access while keeping the patient comfortable and safe. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h2)

question: Why is good communication especially important before doing a vulvar swab?

options.A: The patient must remain completely unconscious during the swab
options.B: Insurance paperwork must be signed while the patient is positioned
options.C: The procedure involves a sensitive and intimate part of the body
options.D: Special medical terminology is required to explain the diagnostic test

explanation: Because this exam is very private, talking calmly with your patient helps ease their nerves and builds great nurse-patient trust. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h2)

question: Why do we use synthetic swab tips (like dacron) instead of regular cotton?

options.A: Synthetic swabs change color to indicate a positive infection
options.B: Cotton can inhibit certain laboratory tests and microbial growth
options.C: Synthetic tips are significantly cheaper to purchase in bulk
options.D: Cotton fibers dissolve completely when exposed to body fluids

explanation: Regular cotton can actually trap or stop germs from growing properly in the lab, so synthetic swabs give us much more reliable test results. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h3)

question: What is the main reason to gather all your equipment before positioning your patient?

options.A: To ensure the laboratory technician is present in the room
options.B: To prevent procedural delays and maintain a smooth workflow
options.C: To keep the examination table warm for the incoming patient
options.D: To fulfill mandatory legal requirements for waste disposal

explanation: Getting your tray ready beforehand means you won't have to leave a vulnerable patient alone while you run off to grab a missing item! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h3)

question: What major mistake should you avoid when collecting a swab sample?

options.A: Using a transport tube that is completely clear of liquid
options.B: Parting the labia majora gently with the non-dominant hand
options.C: Touching the surrounding skin and contaminating the swab
options.D: Rotating the swab against the surface of the lesion too long

explanation: Be careful! Touching normal skin introduces random bacteria that can mess up the test and hide the real cause of the infection. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T15#GNS221_U2_T15_h4)

question: You need to collect a swab from a visible ulcer on the labia minora. What is the correct way to do it?

options.A: Scrape the lesion until it bleeds profusely to get cells
options.B: Press the swab deeply into the underlying muscle tissue
options.C: Rotate the swab firmly across the base of the ulcer
options.D: Rinse the ulcer thoroughly with sterile water first
